newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: U.S. discusses WTO, trade deficit with China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. discusses WTO, trade deficit with China.

text.p: U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky met Chinese counterpart Wu Yi on Thursday to discuss China's burgeoning trade deficit with the United States and its possible membership in the World Trade Organisation.

"Minister Wu and I discussed a wide range of issues, including WTO and the trade deficit," Barshefsky told reporters after the hour-long meeting on the sidelines of the annual Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference.
"We agreed with respect to both issues, as well as bilateral issues, that we would continue to hold productive and mutually beneficial talks," Barshevsky said in brief remarks.
Wu, the Chinese minister of foreign trade and economic cooperation, did not comment.
But a spokesman for the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Economic Cooperation in Beijing said: "The two sides should avoid taking actions that do not help the expansion of trade.
"These are two of the biggest markets in the world. They should be complementary."
The United States said Wednesday its trade deficit with China climbed to nearly $29 billion in the first nine months of the year, from $25 billion in the same period last year.

It also said that in September the deficit with China was $4.73 billion, bigger than with any other country. The third-quarter deficit with China grew to $13.3 billion, exceeding the $11.9 billion gap with Japan.
American economists said the mounting deficit was likely to create new friction between the two countries -- including one over China's bid to join the World Trade Organisation.
China has applied to join the WTO on favourable terms given to developing countries, but Washington has insisted that China's economy was too big for this treatment.
U.S. Undersecretary of State Joan Spero told Reuters Financial Television Thursday the United States wants to see China join the trade body on "commercially meaningful terms."
"What that means is that China has to conform to WTO rules and processes," she said, adding that China must also open up its markets further.
"We very much want this to happen," she said of China's eventual membership in WTO.

The two countries are also in dispute over a U.S. initiative to free global trade in computers and telecommunications, a business that Spero said is worth $1.8 trillion. China opposes it, delegates said.

"APEC operates very much on a consensus," Spero said. "One country doesn't have to sign on. ... But it's very hard for that country to block it when there's a broad consensus and when that country isn't part of the WTO," she said.
President Clinton will meet his Chinese counterpart, Jiang Zemin, in a high-profile bilateral meeting in Manila Sunday, and trade is likely to be one of the main issues discussed.
